name: Observability & Debuggability

checks.check: Operational logs use the project’s structured event/correlation contract where cross-step diagnosis requires it; product/CLI output need not all be JSON.
Core paths (auth, billing, generation, data mutation) expose sufficient correlated success/failure observations through logs, traces or metrics to diagnose the promised behavior.
Unexpected errors include relevant stack/cause and sanitized context; do not expose secrets or unnecessary personal data to logs or public responses.
No PII or secrets in logs
Every request/task has a trackable ID (`trace_id`, `x-request-id`, `run_id`)
Production does NOT rely solely on unstructured `console.log`
Background jobs/workers produce unique `run_id` per execution
External dependency calls log: response time, status code, retry count
Failure paths have explicit instrumentation (not just generic error log)
Log event names are specific and stable (no `something happened`)
Production failures have diagnostic evidence appropriate to the operational needs; identify concrete gaps instead of promising every cause can be known without reproduction.
Verify that promised observability events/trace identifiers reach their intended emit path and are observed; generated names or wrappers are valid when traceable, and grep alone is not runtime proof.
High-risk flows have alert rules — critical paths (auth failure spikes, payment errors, data mutation failures) trigger automated alerts [SHOULD]
Where latency/causality diagnosis requires tracing, important operations emit spans with timing and relevant safe metadata [SHOULD].
Cross-service requests are traceable end-to-end — trace IDs propagate across service boundaries for full request lifecycle visibility [SHOULD]
Logs are retained and accessible to the responsible operators with appropriate access control; use external aggregation where the deployment requires it [SHOULD].
For a user-facing frontend, assess whether real-user performance/failure monitoring is required by operational needs and permitted by privacy constraints.
External dependency monitoring — when project depends on third-party services
A deployed service has a usable health/readiness observation appropriate to its host; it need not always be an HTTP endpoint.
Background and worker paths can answer: did it start, did it run twice, which step failed, and did checkpoint, retry and cleanup behave as intended.
Logs distinguish provider failure from local failure.
Trace context propagates consistently through the supported request/job boundaries, using middleware or an equivalent shared mechanism.
External writes leave an audit trail: actor, timestamp, trace id.

anti_patterns: Unstructured logs as only observability source
No correlation ID / trace ID across related events
Reactive-only debugging (add instrumentation only after incident)
High-risk paths with no visibility into inputs, outputs, failures
PII or secrets leaked in logs
Stub-as-proof: Step 5 commands_run 經 stub / placeholder ID / signature inspection / harness probe / low-level helper 旁路 production entrypoint，取代 truth-owner read-back → flag P1
Where surface proof requires a schema check, verify its actual invocation and result; an absent check is missing proof, and severity follows the affected contract
